title: TB8-00679
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated September 15, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated September 15, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The RPD concluded that the Appellant was not credible and did not believe his fear of persecution by his family, based on his refusal to be a chief priest, or the Nigerian police, due to the sexual orientation of his wife. The Appellant does not submit new evidence under section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or request a hearing under section 110(6). The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

According to his Basis of Claim Form (BOC)1 the Appellant was born in 1972 in XXXX, Nigeria. The Appellant grew up in a family of traditional worshippers who are also Muslims. He attended mosques and occasionally visited the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in his father's home town, XXXX XXXX, in Ogun State. The Appellant went to college in XXXX, married and had four children, his wife ran a XXXX business and he worked as a freight forwarder. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 the Appellant's Uncle XXXX called from the family compound in XXXX XXXX to tell him that his Uncle XXXX, the Chief Priest of the XXXX XXXX had died and that the oracle had chosen the Appellant as the next chief priest. When the Appellant said he was Muslim and it was not possible for him to be the chief priest, his uncle said that he had no choice in the matter and that he must appear before the XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2017 to commence the initiation ritual. The Appellant said no and cut off the conversation.

On XXXX XXXX, 2017 the Appellant got a letter from the XXXX family saying that the first stage of the initiation would take place on XXXX XXXX, 2017 despite the Appellant's objections. The Appellant took the letter to two police stations where he was told that the police do not get involved in matters of religion and family affairs. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 the Appellant was forcefully taken from his home by four men who put him a van and took him to XXXX XXXX where he was forced to participate in the initiation ceremony which involved swearing oaths and drinking a concoction that made him sick. After the initiation the Appellant was returned home. He went to the police again but got no help. Two days later the Appellant got a call from his uncle saying that the final initiation would take place on XXXX, XXXX XXXX, 2017 and that he must attend with his wife and daughter who would be circumcised to complete the process. His uncle threatened to track down and kill the Appellant and his family if he refused to complete the initiation. At this point the Appellant's wife revealed to him that she was bisexual and was being blackmailed by the boyfriend of a past lover. The Appellant decided that they had to leave Nigeria. They already had visas so they came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The Appellant's family's claim for refugee protection was received on May 17, 2017. At the first hearing on July 10, 2017 the Appellant advised that he had separated from his wife and children and he wanted his claim heard separately. He also advised of his second fear of returning to Nigeria because his wife's bisexuality has been reported to the police who are now looking for the Appellant and his wife. A second hearing was held on August 21, 2017. The RPD rendered its decision on September 15, 2017 finding that the Appellant was not a credible witness.

The RAD reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts a standard of review of reasonableness adapted to the RAD. 2 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.
The determinative issue is whether or not the RPD erred when it found that the Appellant is not credible.

In finding the Appellant was not credible the RPD cited the following reasons in its decision:3 - Without documentary evidence or a photograph the Appellant did not establish that his family worshipped idols at the XXXX XXXX; - The Appellant was not able to state when his Uncle XXXX, the late Chief Priest, had died; - The Appellant did not present any documentary evidence about the death of the Chief Priest or his relation to the Chief Priest; - The Appellant did not present any documentary evidence about the existence of, or his relation to, the Uncle XXXX who forced him to the first initiation and threated to harm him if he failed to become the chief priest; - The hospital report and newspaper article submitted by the Appellant were not genuine; - The psychological report submitted by the Appellant does not confirm that his post-traumatic stress disorder is related to what he was allegedly subjected to in Nigeria; - The Appellant's contradictory evidence about his wife's sexuality (bisexual vs. lesbian) without explanation; - The absence of any evidence of the Appellant's wife's same-sex partner; - The absence of any evidence of the boyfriend of the Appellant's wife's same-sex partner or any documentary evidence such as media or police reports to indicate that the boyfriend had reported the Appellant's wife and her same-sex partner to the Nigerian police; and, - The affidavit from the Appellant's friend is fabricated for the purpose of the refugee claim.

The Appellant argues that the RPD made a negative credibility finding based on an incorrect assessment of the evidence, lack of corroboration and its fixation on tangential and peripheral issues. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred when it did not believe the Appellant's testimony without alleging inconsistencies and basing its findings solely on conjecture, implausibility and lack of corroboration. The Appellant reviews each of the reasons identified by the RPD for finding him not credible and says they were made in error.
I have considered each of Appellant's arguments and I have undertaken my own independent assessment of the evidence and testimony.

I agree with the Appellant that the RPD's credibility assessment did not strictly comply with jurisprudential principles as recently laid out by the Federal Court4 and was not, therefore, sufficient to support its finding. The RPD did not adequately identify the accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's testimony so it relied too heavily on the absence of corroborative evidence. As detailed below I have undertaken my own analysis to supplement that of the RPD and find that the Appellant is not credible. RAD credibility analysis

Following my independent analysis I identified numerous problems with the Appellant's evidence relating to the central elements of his claim: his family will harm him because he refused to become the chief priest; and, the police in Nigeria are looking for him because his wife is a lesbian. Chief priest
There are a number of inconsistencies, contradictions and omissions in the Appellant's story that his family is forcing him to be the chief priest and will kill him because he refused.

Objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) contradicts the evidence of the Appellant that his family would force him to take the position of chief priest. In the Response to Information Request (RIR) entitled Consequences for a person to refuse a chief priest or fetish priest position for which they have been selected in south and central Nigeria,5 experts from the African Studies Centre at the University of Leiden (AFC), the University of London (London) and Franklin & Marshall College (F&M) state the following: * It would not be considered an offense against the shrine for someone to refuse the role of chief priest or fetish priest (AFC); * Research indicates that there are no consequence for someone who refuses a position of chief priest or fetish priest (London); * He had never heard of the priesthood being forced on anyone in Nigeria (AFC); * The shrine would want a successor who had the interest and aptitude for the role (AFC); * The successor would likely be initiated at a young age (AFC); * Christians have been refusing to take their inherited offices in shrines since the beginning of Christian missionization in Nigeria-that is since the middle of the 19th century (F&M).

The Appellant's evidence about his refusal to take the position is not consistent. In his BOC the Appellant says that during a telephone call on XXXX XXXX, 2017 he told his uncles that he could not be the chief priest because he is a Muslim, "I said 'no' and cut off the conversation." Also in his BOC the Appellant references a telephone call received from an uncle two days after his first initiation (XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX, 2017) threatening the Appellant and his family with death if he did not complete the process. This is inconsistent with the tone of the letters received from the Appellant's uncle on XXXX XXXX, 2017 (XXXX XXXX, 2017 Letter) 6 and XXXX XXXX, 2017 (XXXX XXXX, 2017 Letter)7 which do not reference the Appellant's refusal or make any threats and respectively end with "[o]nce again, congratulations on your new appointment and we hope you have a great and successful tenure" and "[a]gain, congratulations and we look forward to handing over the staff of power to you."

There are other credibility issues with the XXXX XXXX, 2017 Letter and the XXXX XXXX, 2017 Letter. They are both on letterhead which has a significant spelling error, "Decendants" instead of "Descendants." The Appellant's BOC says he received the letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2017 from his uncle in XXXX XXXX on the same day in Lagos. The XXXX XXXX, 2017 references the circumcision of the Appellant's wife and daughter which is illegal in Nigeria.8

Objective evidence in the NDP also contradicts the Appellant's evidence about the ritual practices in Yorubaland9 which includes Ogun State where XXXX XXXX is located. In his BOC the Appellant says that during his initiation he would be made to "eat the heart and flesh of a human being." The objective evidence says human sacrifice is against the law of Nigeria and anyone caught practicing human sacrifice would be severely dealt and perpetrators will be arrested.

The Appellant says that his wife and daughter were going to be circumcised as part of his initiation as chief priest. There is nothing in the NDP that speaks to this being a ritual practice associated with the initiation of a chief priest. As noted above the NDP10 does make it clear that female genital mutilation (FGM) has been prohibited nationwide since May 2015 and had already been banned in Ogun State.

The Appellant's BOC says that he was forcefully taken from his home and driven to XXXX XXXX for the first part of the initiation ceremony on XXXX XXXX, 2017. This directly contradicts the statement early in his BOC and the XXXX XXXX, 2017 Letter which said that the initiation was going to be held on XXXX XXXX, 2017. The Appellant testified that he was picked up in the morning and returned the same night.11

The Appellant's BOC says that he was forced to drink a concoction during the ceremony that make him feel sick. After the initiation the Appellant's BOC says he was returned home and went again to the police for help. The Appellant submitted a medical report dated XXXX XXXX, 2107 (Medical Report)12 which states that he admitted to hospital on XXXX XXXX, 2017 "with history of physical assault, severe stomach pain and query food poison that involved unlawful initiation ceremony and drinking of a concoction" and that he was discharged on XXXX XXXX, 2017. The Appellant's BOC does not reference either the hospitalization or the assault. When asked about this significant omission at the hearing the Appellant said that "it was not assault as in beating, it was roughed up."13

I also noted a number of issues on the face of the Medical Report including: a typographical error in the letterhead "Chek-up" instead of "Check-up"; the wet seal appears to be beneath the signature of the author and is not readable; it does not use medical language; does not detail the laboratory tests or scans undertaken; and, provides no details of the treatment given during the Appellant's five days of hospitalization.

The Appellant's BOC says that two days after he returned following the initiation (XXXX XXXX or XXXX, 2017) he got a call from one of his uncles saying the final initiation would take place on XXXX, XXXX XXXX, 2017 and that he and his family would be killed if he did not complete the initiation. This contradicts the Appellant's testimony as he says that he was incapacitated on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and hospitalized from that date until XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The Appellant's BOC says that he came to the conclusion that he had to leave Nigeria after the first phase of the initiation, which took place on either XXXX XXXX, 2017 or XXXX XXXX, 2017, and the threats made against his family two days later. This is inconsistent with the support letter from his friend14 which said that the Appellant brought luggage to his house on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and asked him to keep it without explanation.

I find that this accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies and omissions regarding crucial elements of the Appellant's claim lead to a negative conclusion about his credibility, sufficient to reverse the presumption of truthfulness. My negative credibility finding is supported by the absence of corroborative evidence identified by the RPD as detailed above. I agree with the RPD that corroborative evidence should have been reasonably available to establish essential elements of a claim and the Appellant did not have a reasonable explanation for its absence.

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant has not established that he was named chief priest following the death of his uncle, that he attended a first initiation ceremony and was hospitalized afterwards and that his uncles threatened him and his family with death if he refused the position. Wife's sexuality

The Appellant's fear of persecution because he was told that the Nigerian police are looking for his wife because of her bisexual behaviour is referenced briefly in his amended BOC:15 I now have additional fear of returned to Nigeria because I was told that the Police are now looking for my wife and me because her bisexual behavior has now been reported to the Police and the Police have visited our home looking for my wife and I.

During his hearing the Appellant's testimony was not very clear or consistent. At one point he said that he feared the police in Nigeria because "When we left the place, my wife was dating a woman... My wife is a lesbian...So the police officer came to the house and they were looking for me as well."16 This is not consistent with the Appellant's BOC which only referenced his wife's previous relationships with women and does not mention that his wife was dating a woman when they left Nigeria.

In his BOC the Appellant said that his wife was being blackmailed by "the boyfriend of her past lover who came into possession of sex tapes and naked suggestive photographs of her and her previous girlfriend." This is not consistent with the Appellant's testimony that his wife was being blackmailed by this "other guy" who the girl his wife was sleeping with in university had married and this "other guy" had found some pictures of them sleeping together.17

The Appellant did not identify the alleged blackmailer who reported his wife to the police in his BOC or amended BOC. In his testimony the Appellant could only identify him by his first name, said that he did not know him, had not seen him and was just told by his wife.18

As noted by the RPD the Appellant said in his BOC that his wife is bisexual and his testimony was that his wife is lesbian. When asked about this contradiction the Appellant's response was not coherent.

These contradictions, inconsistencies and omission, combined with the total absence of any corroborative evidence as detailed above by the RPD, lead me to conclude that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities that the police are looking for him due to his wife's sexuality.

The Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he is under threat of death from his family for refusing the position of chief priest or that he is wanted by the authorities in Cameroon due to his wife's sexuality. As such, he has neither established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution in Cameroon, nor that on a balance of probabilities he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Cameroon.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
